operations.name: John Vilarino

expected.name: John Vilarino
expected.description: John Vilarino was born in La Coruña, Spain, on January 1, 1885, and first came to the United States in 1903. A Los Angeles restaurant worker, he was married with eleven children. Police arrested him at Communist Party headquarters on February 26, 1930 on suspicion of criminal syndicalism. Immigration authorities then sought his deportation because of his Communist affiliation and political literature. He was detained in the Los Angeles County Jail during the immigration proceedings. Vilarino was also arrested during the May Day demonstration that year. Attorney John Beardsley challenged the deportation order, but the Ninth Circuit affirmed it on June 8, 1931. The International Labor Defense subsequently secured a one-year postponement of deportation.

operations.name: Emma Cutler

expected.name: Emma Cutler
expected.description: Emma Cutler was a Los Angeles Communist organizer and secretary of the Los Angeles Workers’ School. She was sentenced to ninety days in the Los Angeles County Jail and a $500 fine for taking part in the August 1, 1930, anti-imperialist demonstration. In 1936, she ran for Congress in California’s 13th District against incumbent Charles Kramer. On July 11, police arrested her while she spoke at a Communist Party street meeting on Echo Park Boulevard. They held her at police headquarters for about an hour and released her that night. As an International Labor Defense organizer, she defended arrested agricultural workers in the San Joaquin and Imperial valleys. In 1934, while investigating the arrests of lettuce strikers, she was arrested for vagrancy and served six months in the El Centro jail. She appealed her conviction and sought habeas corpus relief. Her confinement included a release on a writ followed by a return to jail.

operations.name: Victor Aronson

expected.name: Victor Aronson
expected.description: Victor Aronson was a labor-defense organizer arrested in the late-1929 crackdown on seamen's organizing in New Orleans. Authorities accused him of sedition over the distribution of the Labor Defender and union leaflets. The International Labor Defense and attorney R. A. Darling secured the release of the four New Orleans defendants, including Aronson, and dismissal of their charges by December 25, 1929.
expected.body:
1920s remaining-entry review: The November 29, 1929 Daily Worker, page 2, column 3, individually names Victor Aronson and William J. Davis as the Marine Workers League organizers arrested Monday while distributing leaflets and Marine Workers Voices near the New Orleans cotton mills. The article begins on page 1 with a November 28 dateline, making Monday November 25. The full page 2 scan was visually checked by the research agent. This was the earlier paired arrest, distinct from the subsequent headquarters arrests of Morgan and Brown. Davis is the spelling in this original report; the imported Davids identity spelling is noted but not changed or merged here. Only the arrest date is corrected; existing release precision and unresolved admission are not inferred from it.

Source

operations.name: George Saul

expected.name: George Saul
expected.description: George J. Saul organized Southern textile workers for the National Textile Workers Union and worked for the International Labor Defense. He was jailed in Gaston County after police broke up his November 1929 speech at Mount Holly and was released on bail on November 24. Saul received a six-month chain-gang sentence during the Southern organizing campaign. A new trial was granted in 1930. That July he joined the Communist League of America (Opposition) and announced that he would return south for trial. He had also worked with Hugo Oehler in the Colorado coal strike.

operations.name: Solomon Harper

expected.name: Solomon Harper
expected.description: Solomon Harper was a labor organizer, and famed inventor who created the electric hair roller along with over two dozen other inventions. He organized with the American Negro Labor Congress and International Labor Defense and belonged to the Workers Ex-Servicemen's League. In 1930, police arrested and beat him after he called for prosecution against the people responsible for lynching Georgia Pullman porter J. H. Wilkins at a Brotherhood of Sleeping Car Porters meeting in New York. He was charged with inciting-to-riot and disorderly-conduct and received a three-month jail sentence. After his release he continued campaigning against lynching and for unemployment relief and veterans' benefits.

operations.name: Cliff Saylors

expected.name: Cliff Saylors
expected.description: Cliff Saylors was a textile worker and Southern organizer for the International Labor Defense during the Gastonia strike cases. After the December 1929 ILD conference in Charlotte, North Carolina, authorities issued a warrant accusing him of the murder of Gastonia police chief Orville Aderholt. Saylors was arrested and jailed on January 7, 1930. The state dropped the murder charge for lack of evidence on January 13, minutes after his lawyers obtained a writ of habeas corpus, and he was released at 8 p.m. A separate perjury charge remained pending.

operations.name: Jessie Wakefield

expected.name: Jessie Wakefield
expected.description: Jessie London Wakefield was an International Labor Defense field representative who organized legal defense and relief for jailed coal miners in Harlan County, Kentucky, in 1931. Her car was dynamited while she was carrying food and clothing to miners’ families. She was arrested on criminal-syndicalism charges, released on $2,000 bail, and then arrested again. After a hearing on August 10, Judge Whitehead held her for the grand jury with $5,000 bail and an additional $5,000 peace bond. She was confined in the Harlan County jail alongside Civil Liberties Union representative Arnold Johnson. By September 13, both had been released on condition that they leave Harlan County. Wakefield left the Kentucky organizing field on September 12 and subsequently worked as secretary of the ILD Prisoners’ Relief Fund.

operations.name: Mike Kulikoff

expected.name: Mike Kulikoff
expected.description: Mike Kulikoff was an eighteen-year-old Portland high-school student and Young Communist League member who was confined in the Oregon State Hospital in Salem after efforts to deport him to the Soviet Union failed. He entered the hospital on November 8, 1930. His father, Alex, sought his release through a habeas corpus proceeding, and both his father and brother William joined the International Labor Defense. Kulikoff remained confined in February 1931 while an appeal was pending before the Oregon Supreme Court. He was later paroled following a protest campaign.

operations.name: Fred Firestone

expected.name: Fred Firestone
expected.description: Fred Firestone was a Los Angeles labor organizer and secretary of the city's International Labor Defense branch. He directed local election-campaign work in 1930 and was jailed in 1931 for speaking at a factory-gate meeting. The International Labor Defense included him in its campaign for imprisoned workers.

operations.name: John Della Monica

expected.name: John Della Monica
expected.description: John Della Monica led the International Labor Defense in Utica, New York. He and four other unemployed workers were prosecuted after a demonstration demanding relief. Their December 1932 trial resulted in convictions, and Della Monica and Communist organizer Peter Kraus received sentences of one and a half to three years at Auburn State Prison. The International Labor Defense appealed the convictions and sought a new trial.

operations.name: John Soderberg

expected.name: John Soderberg
expected.description: John G. Soderberg was born in Stockholm, Sweden, on June 12, 1895. He was secretary-treasurer of the Independent Tidewater Boatmen's Union in New York Harbor and had worked as an International Labor Defense organizer in 1930 and 1931. He was arrested with other boatmen in November 1931 after police alleged a conspiracy to bomb barges. From the Tombs, he maintained that the defendants were innocent and were being prosecuted for organizing workers. On April 25, 1932, he was sentenced to twelve and a half to twenty-five years for placing explosives in a vessel. He served his prison term at Sing Sing, where he was numbered 85978. He was paroled on January 6, 1942, and deported to Sweden aboard the S.S. Danaholm the following day.

operations.name: Alice Burke

expected.name: Alice Burke
expected.description: Alice Burke, born Alice Phillips in Montana in 1909, was a Communist and Unemployed Council organizer in Birmingham, Alabama. She and Wirt Taylor were arrested on November 7, 1932, after leading a relief demonstration of Black and white unemployed workers. She was convicted in the city recorder’s court and again in circuit court on May 9, 1933. On June 5, the court imposed a $100 fine, 100 days of hard labor for failure to pay it and another 150 days of hard labor. While held in Jefferson County Jail, Burke wrote about its food, sanitation and treatment of prisoners. The International Labor Defense furnished $2,000 bond, securing her and Taylor’s release on July 24, 1933, pending appeal. She later ran as a Communist candidate for the U.S. Senate and governor of Virginia.

operations.name: Alexander Racolin

expected.name: Alexander Racolin
expected.description: Alexander Racolin was a New York attorney and International Labor Defense organizer active in the South. Birmingham police arrested him with Laura Stark during a warrantless raid on the ILD office on May 9, 1934, and released him about an hour later without charges. DeKalb County officers arrested him on October 14 during a private meeting at Mrs. R. W. Alling’s home, where Clarence Weaver reported on an anti-war congress. Held under Georgia’s insurrection law, Racolin remained in custody until November 3, when the grand jury refused to indict him and he was released unconditionally.

operations.name: George Kaplan

expected.name: George Kaplan
expected.description: George Kaplan was an International Labor Defense organizer jailed during the 1933 Gallup coal strike in New Mexico. A military court sentenced him to six months in Albuquerque under the martial law imposed on the strike. Kaplan and unemployed-workers' organizer Herbert Benjamin were beaten in the Gallup jail; miners demonstrated outside to demand their freedom. Jailers later tried to make the three sentenced organizers agree to leave New Mexico for a year. They refused. Continued strike action secured their unconditional release in November 1933.

operations.name: Ripley Gibson

expected.name: Ripley Gibson
expected.description: Ripley Gibson was a member of the Scottsboro branch of the International Labor Defense in Denver. During the October 30, 1934 relief workers’ strike, police clubbed him unconscious and arrested him. The strike opposed relief cuts and sought a thirty-hour week at union wages. The International Labor Defense obtained bail for sixteen defendants and organized their defense against riot and related charges, with trial scheduled for December 11.

operations.name: Whirlwind Larson

expected.name: Whirlwind Larson
expected.description: Whirlwind Larson was a Chicago salesman for the Daily Worker and Sunday Worker who had immigrated to the United States in 1904. His attempts to obtain citizenship failed amid his labor activity and financial difficulties. After applying for permission to re-enter the country in 1934, he was summoned to a federal office, recognized as a labor-paper salesman, handcuffed and taken to the county jail for deportation proceedings. Larson was arrested at noon on a Thursday and freed at noon on Saturday after the International Labor Defense raised $1,000 cash bail. He then pledged to organize a neighborhood defense branch and raise money for other imprisoned workers.

operations.name: William Fisher

expected.name: William Fisher
expected.description: William Fisher was an International Labor Defense member in Niagara Falls, New York. On August 27, 1934, a gang attacked a defense meeting for Alphonse Davis, a Black worker facing a rape prosecution. Fisher tried to protect two women at the meeting and was severely injured. He was placed under arrest while hospitalized with cuts and a possible skull fracture. A jury convicted him of assault and battery on October 25. He received an indeterminate sentence of two and a half to five years, which the International Labor Defense appealed. He remained imprisoned in December 1935.

operations.name: Joe Bartol

expected.name: Joe Bartol
expected.description: Joe Bartol was a Gallup coal miner and president of the Southwestern mine's union local. During the 1933 strike the National Guard confined him in a military stockade, released him after three days and arrested him again after he began organizing food relief. He remained in the stockade until the strike ended. Bartol later became an International Labor Defense secretary and helped bring National Miners Union locals into the United Mine Workers of America. After the April 1935 confrontation in Gallup, he was imprisoned in the New Mexico State Penitentiary at Santa Fe under $7,500 murder bail. He was acquitted in the October trial but remained detained on the separate charge of aiding a prisoner to escape. His wife Julia campaigned for the prisoners' defense.

operations.name: Gregorio Correa

expected.name: Gregorio Correa
expected.description: Gregorio Correa was a Gallup coal miner and father of six. During the 1933 strike he distributed food through the strike relief committee, picketed and was arrested while urging another miner to join the walkout. He later worked on CWA and FERA relief projects and joined the 1934 relief strike. After the April 1935 confrontation in Gallup, he was held in the New Mexico State Penitentiary at Santa Fe on charges of first-degree murder and aiding a prisoner to escape. Bail was set at $7,500 on the murder charge and another $1,000 on the escape charge. He was acquitted in the Gallup trial.

operations.name: Victorio Correa

expected.name: Victorio Correa
expected.description: Victorio Correa was a coal miner and National Miners Union picket captain in the 1933 Gallup, New Mexico strike. He was wounded in the leg by a strikebreaker or company supporter during that strike. His brothers Alejandro and Gregorio also organized among Gallup miners. Victorio participated in the International Labor Defense, the Unemployed Council and protests for relief work. After the April 4, 1935 confrontation in which Sheriff M. R. Carmichael was killed, he was held in the state penitentiary at Santa Fe and prosecuted with nine other men for murder. The jury acquitted Correa in October, but he was immediately returned to jail under $2,000 bond on a separate accusation of helping a prisoner escape. He also faced deportation proceedings.

operations.name: Rafael Gomez

expected.name: Rafael Gomez
expected.description: Rafael Gomez was a coal miner and labor activist in Gallup, New Mexico. He began working at nine and later worked in a Texas restaurant, for a Los Angeles gas company and in metal and coal mines. He joined the National Miners Union during the 1933 Gallup strike and served on its picket line. He also belonged to the International Labor Defense and Unemployed Councils. In 1934 he was a strike-committee member and picket captain during a Federal Emergency Relief Administration workers' strike. Authorities arrested him after the April 4, 1935, Gallup confrontation in which Sheriff M. R. Carmichael and two miners were killed. Charged with murder and aiding a prisoner's escape, he was held under $7,500 bond. The jury acquitted him of murder in October, but he remained jailed on the aiding-escape charge under $2,500 bond. He also faced deportation to Spain.

operations.name: Lowell Alvin Wakefield

expected.name: Lowell Alvin Wakefield
expected.description: Lowell Alvin Wakefield was a Washington labor journalist and the International Labor Defense’s first Southern organizer. He helped bring national attention to the Scottsboro prosecution in 1931 and organized legal defense for Black and white workers in Alabama. Birmingham police arrested him on August 12, 1931, during raids against Communist organizers; he was jailed during that campaign. Returning to Seattle, he founded and edited the Voice of Action. On July 31, 1935, King County authorities indicted Wakefield and staff member Emerson Daggett for criminal libel after five American Federation of Labor officials complained about the newspaper’s reporting during the Northwest lumber strike. Wakefield later established a major Alaska king-crab fishing business.

operations.name: Carl Ohm

expected.name: Carl Ohm
expected.description: Carl Ohm, also printed as Karl Ohm, legally entered the United States in April 1929. He was an International Labor Defense member arrested during an October 1932 New York demonstration against the persecution of Black people. Immigration officials sought to deport him to Germany, alleging membership in the Communist Party or Young Communist League. He was detained at Ellis Island while the American Committee for Protection of Foreign Born and attorney Irving Schwab fought his case. On November 4, 1935, the Second Circuit reversed the deportation order and directed a new hearing because the immigration inspector who heard the witnesses had not supplied the required findings. The Department of Labor's Board of Review subsequently upheld a deportation order in September 1936.

operations.name: Ray Carlson

expected.name: Ray Carlson
expected.description: Ray Carlson, also reported as Ragnar Carlson, was a Swedish immigrant and International Labor Defense organizer in Spokane, Washington. Immigration authorities detained him in Washington and sent him east from Spokane under guard on a deportation train on October 25, 1934. His wife and young son accompanied him, and he was subsequently held at Ellis Island. He was held in solitary confinement while fighting deportation. Judge Goddard denied habeas corpus petitions for Carlson and fellow detainee John Ujich on December 7, 1934; their lawyers secured a ten-day stay to appeal. The Committee for the Protection of the Foreign Born subsequently obtained Carlson's release on bail, reported by March 28, 1935.

operations.name: Ed Sears

expected.name: Ed Sears
expected.description: Ed Sears was a Black union miner in Bessemer, Alabama, and an International Labor Defense activist. He and fellow Black Communist Nathan Strong were expelled from Mine Mill's Bessemer local because of their political affiliations. In 1935 police took Sears off a trolley, jailed him and denied him access to counsel. Within three hours he was tried and sentenced to ten months on the chain gang and a $100 fine for carrying Sasha Small's Scottsboro pamphlet, Act 3. The International Labor Defense and National Committee for the Defense of Political Prisoners challenged the anti-radical ordinance. Circuit Judge Gardner Goodwin ruled it unconstitutional in September, and Sears was freed.

operations.name: Laura Stark

expected.name: Laura Stark
expected.description: Laura Stark was the Southern district secretary of the International Labor Defense in Birmingham, Alabama. Police arrested her without a warrant at the ILD office on May 9, 1934, during a campaign against Communist and interracial labor organizing. She was jailed and tried on a vagrancy charge before Judge Abernathy on May 17. In court, Stark challenged the use of a racial slur against Black workers, while fellow defendants defended their organizing among Black and white miners.

operations.name: Oreal Grossman

expected.name: Oreal Grossman
expected.description: Oreal Grossman was a Rhode Island civil-liberties attorney born in Providence and trained at Northeastern University. He practiced in Pawtucket and worked with the International Labor Defense and American Civil Liberties Union. On September 13, 1934, during the general textile strike, he went to Providence police headquarters to represent imprisoned workers. Police detained him after questioning him about his political views. He was held incommunicado for thirty-six hours and released on bail on a lottery charge based on his possession of a benefit-banquet ticket.

operations.name: Robert Washington

expected.name: Robert Washington
expected.description: Robert Washington was a Black organizer and local International Labor Defense leader in Alabama. Police jailed him after raiding an ILD picnic outside Birmingham on September 6, 1934. In May 1935, Selma police detained him on vagrancy charges during repression of sharecroppers' organizing. When he left the jail, eight armed men seized him, drove him into the country and flogged him unconscious. In 1936, Birmingham police arrested him for driving a car with defective brakes. The traffic court imposed 180 days on a chain gang and a $100 fine, but he spent eight days in the city jail before the ILD obtained his release on $300 bail pending appeal.
